title: Acids, Bases, pH and Buffers
seo_title: Year 12 Chemistry: Acids, Bases and PH Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, conjugate pairs and amphiprotic species; the self-ionisation of water and Kw; pH of strong acids and bases; weak acids, Ka and pKa; buffers; acid–base titrations, indicators and titration curves. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 3: Equilibrium, acids and redox reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Chemistry worksheets on acids and bases: conjugate pairs, Kw, pH of strong and weak acids, Ka and pKa, buffers, titrations and indicators. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base.
body_html:
How to think about it

An acid donates a proton and its conjugate base can accept one back. Water self-ionises: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14.

Strong acids ionise completely, so [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration (×2 for H₂SO₄). For weak acids use Ka: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka × c). Buffers resist pH change. In a titration the indicator must change colour near the equivalence point.

Example

pH of 0.0010 mol/L KOH?

[OH⁻] = 10⁻³

[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻¹¹

Answer: 11

Example

0.10 mol/L acid, Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. pH?

[H₃O⁺] = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³

Answer: 3

Common mistakes

  • Using [OH⁻] directly in pH = −log[H₃O⁺].
  • Treating a weak acid as fully ionised.
  • Choosing phenolphthalein for a strong acid–weak base titration.

faq.q: Why does a buffer resist pH change?
faq.a: Added H₃O⁺ reacts with the conjugate base, and added OH⁻ reacts with the weak acid, so [H₃O⁺] hardly changes.
Only at 25 °C. Kw changes with temperature, so neutral water is slightly below pH 7 when hot.
